candidates.text:
three gods ruled over the world as supreme rulers. Gombo and Kagotsuch said they would create life in the clouds as only they could. Gombo created life in the ocean, as was fit for him. Saguchi would have made the life of the plants, but Gombo grew jealous and told Kagotsuch and Saguchi to go away.

And so they did. They left their master, alone, but not forgotten. Gombo created many people, but his jealousy caused his creations to become afraid and chaotic. In response, he grew angry, disorganized and developed a temper; all of which was reflected in his created world.

Saguchi and Kagotsuch were never satisfied with a life spent apart from their brothers. It was so empty. So lifeless. And so…

Their plan was to wake their brother Gombo and fool him into leaving his universe to go find them. Once he left, they could go take over his world. However, their plan backfired, and they arrived before their brother, finding himself bored and directionless. Gombo told his brothers that he was stuck in this world until he met his soulmate, and it was an impossible task. Their brother requested they stay there with him.

They followed their order and waited. However, it was not long before Gombo's temper and untouchable ego grew too much to stand and the two left their brother, returning to the world he created for them.

humans lived in a massive palace, only a wall, Aether or Void, separated them from the land. There humans built their palace and had their power. It is said that any soul could enter their palace, no matter what their status. However, when humans built their palace, they began to kill their own, until the last soldier of the Royal Guard killed the human king and allowed the entire population to move to the core of the capital. They gifted the Royal Guard his ring, to allow him to move back and forth between the palace and the core.

Long ago in Lanigami, King Akarikazu, ruler of all humans, ordered his Royal Guard to search for an ancient myth, said to take place on the small peninsula of Mount Aino in the east. The Royal Guard was ordered to bring back the stone, said to take the form of a metal clay, black and slightly silver. It was no use, and when the Royal Guard returned to report, King Akarikazu was furious, and so the King and his Royal Guard changed through a portal to the other side of the wall, that separates Lanigami from The Realms of Concordia.

The Royal Guard found the clay, and but in part it into his ring.

Over time, the Royal Guard was named, Diamond, and he experimented. He designed costumes, moving to the far west to build his kingdom of garb, and chipped away some of the blue jewel.

# The Genesis of Lanigami

The world of Lanigami is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning, there was only the Fold—an infinite, shimmering plane of parchment-white void that bent and creased upon itself in endless silence. No stars burned. No waters stirred. There was only the quiet rustling of potential, like pages turning in an empty room.

From the deepest crease of the Fold, two beings emerged: **Orika**, who was shaped like an open hand, and **Suumeth**, who was shaped like a closed fist. They were not born, nor created—they simply *unfolded*, as if they had always existed within the material of the void, waiting only for the proper crease to reveal them.

Orika spoke first, and her voice was the sound of tearing. Where her words fell, the Fold ripped open, and from the wounds poured color—deep reds and burning golds and the blue-black of bruised sky. She laughed at what she had done, and her laughter made the tears spread wider, and the colors bled and pooled into what would become the seas and skies and molten hearts of mountains.

Suumeth did not speak. Instead, he pressed his closed fist against the Fold and *pushed*, compressing the void until it became dense and heavy and real. Where Orika tore open, Suumeth pressed together. From his pressure came stone and bone and iron. From his silence came gravity, the weight that taught all things to fall.

Together—though they did not intend it—their acts of tearing and pressing created the first land. It rose jagged and wet from the colored void, folded upon itself like a crumpled letter, and this is why the geography of Lanigami is as it is: mountains that bend at impossible angles, valleys that tuck beneath themselves, rivers that flow upward along creased ridges before spilling into inverted lakes. The world was not built—it was *folded into being*.

But the land was empty, and this troubled the being called **Thessaly**, who had not emerged from a crease at all but from the *shadow* cast when Orika and Suumeth first stood opposite one another. Thessaly was neither hand nor fist but something in between—fingers half-curled, as if holding something invisible. She was the Third, the Unintended, and she is sometimes called the God Between the Paper.

Thessaly walked the folded land and found it beautiful but lonely. So she did what neither Orika nor Suumeth could do: she **wrote**.

From her half-curled fingers, she drew symbols in the air—not words of any language, but shapes that *wanted* to mean something. The first symbol she drew became the **Oru**, great winged serpents of living ink who swam through the newborn skies and whose shed scales became the first forests. The second symbol became the **Tessik**, small and clever creatures of folded stone who burrowed into the mountains and learned, over long ages, to stand upright and think. The third symbol she began but never finished—her hand trembled, the line went crooked, and from that broken symbol poured the **Unwritten**, formless things of half-intent that crept into the spaces between folds and have haunted Lanigami ever since.

Orika saw what Thessaly had done and was delighted, for she loved all things that were new. She blessed the living things with passion, with hunger, with the desire to tear open the unknown and find what lay within. This is why mortals are curious. This is why they are restless.

Suumeth saw what Thessaly had done and was troubled, for he feared that which he could not compress into order. He laid down the **Three Creases of Law**: that all living things must age, that all built things must eventually fall, and that no being—mortal or divine—may unfold the world back into the void. In the beginning,

candidates.text:
there was no earth, no sky, and no sea—only a darkness so old it had forgotten what it was hiding.

Within that darkness slept a creature called Nami, whose body had no end. When Nami dreamed, its dreams became colors; when it stirred, those colors tangled together. But there was nothing to see them, and so they faded.

For an age beyond counting, Nami dreamed alone.

Then, one night—for nights existed before days—a dream refused to disappear.

It was a small, silver moth.

The moth settled upon Nami’s brow and asked, “Why do you make beautiful things only to lose them?”

“Because there is nowhere to keep them,” Nami answered.

“Then make somewhere.”

Nami opened one eye.

Where its gaze fell, the darkness hardened into stone. Where its breath passed, the stone softened into earth. It shook the dust from its skin, and the dust became stars. Yet the world lay cold and empty beneath them.

The moth flew downward and struck the earth with its wings.

From the first stroke came the mountains.

From the second came the forests.

From the third came every creature that walks, burrows, crawls, or hides beneath a leaf.

But with each stroke, the moth grew smaller.

Nami saw what was happening and wept. Its tears filled the valleys, making rivers and seas.

In the beginning, there was no earth, no sky, and no sea—only a darkness so old it had forgotten what it was hiding.

Within that darkness slept a creature called Nami, whose body had no end. When Nami dreamed, its dreams became colors; when it stirred, those colors tangled together. But there was nothing to see them, and so they faded.

For an age beyond counting, Nami dreamed alone.

Then, one night—for nights existed before days—a dream refused to disappear.

It was a small, silver moth.

The moth settled upon Nami’s brow and asked, “Why do you make beautiful things only to lose them?”

“Because there is nowhere to keep them,” Nami answered.

“Then make somewhere.”

Nami opened one eye.

Where its gaze fell, the darkness hardened into stone. Where its breath passed, the stone softened into earth. It shook the dust from its skin, and the dust became stars. Yet the world lay cold and empty beneath them.

The moth flew downward and struck the earth with its wings.

From the first stroke came the mountains.

From the second came the forests.

From the third came every creature that walks, burrows, crawls, or hides beneath a leaf.

But with each stroke, the moth grew smaller.

Nami saw what was happening and wept. Its tears filled the valleys, making rivers and seas. Its grief warmed the waters, and from them rose the first clouds.

“Stop,” Nami begged. “You will vanish.”

“Not if there is somewhere to keep me,” said the moth.

With its last strength, it struck the heavens.

Its wings broke into two great lights: one golden and fierce, the other silver and watchful. Its body scattered into countless sparks, which entered the creatures below and taught them to dream.

This is why the sun gives warmth, the moon gives wonder, and all living things carry something they cannot name.

Nami gathered the new world against its breast and called it **Lanigami**, which in the first language meant *the place where a dream is kept*.

Then it lay down beneath the earth to sleep once more.

The first people were born much later, from reeds growing beside the oldest river. They emerged without names, without stories, and without fear. For a time, they lived happily, eating fruit and drinking rain, but they could not remember one day from another. When someone wandered away, those who remained soon forgot them.

One evening, the moon descended to the riverbank in the shape of a pale woman. She placed a clay bowl among the reeds and told the people to speak into it.

One named the river.

Another named the trees.

A third named a child who had gone missing.

The bowl filled with water, though no rain had fallen. On its surface appeared the child, asleep beneath a distant cedar. The people found him and carried him home.

After that, they named their children, their villages, their dead, and the paths between them. They kept bowls beside their hearths and told stories over the water.

But the pale woman warned them, “A name will help you keep a thing. It will not keep it unchanged.”

Then she returned to the sky.

So the people of Lanigami learned to remember—and, more slowly, to let go.

They say Nami still dreams beneath the mountains. Sometimes its dreams rise through the soil as flowers no one has seen before, or animals that speak only once, or doors appearing in the trunks of ancient trees. Earthquakes are its restless movements. Hot springs are the warmth of its breath.

And when a silver moth enters a house at night, no one drives it away.

They set a bowl of water beside the window, leave room for it near the lamp, and tell it something worth keeping.

candidates.text:
there was only the Great Void, an endless expanse of silence and stillness. From this nothingness emerged the Primordial Serpent, Nagaía, whose scales shimmered with the colors of all the worlds yet to be. Nagaía coiled through the Void, weaving dreams and possibilities with each graceful movement.

As Nagaía danced, her scales began to shed, and from each fallen scale, a Starborn emerged. These Starborn were the first beings of Lanigami, luminous entities composed of pure light and potential. They hovered in the darkness, whispering secrets to one another, their voices forming the first echoes of creation.

From Nagaía's breath came the winds of change, which spun the Starborn into a grand constellation. Each Starborn took its place in the Celestial Tapestry, defining the bounds of the cosmos. As the tapestry grew, the first hint of sound returned to the Void—a gentle hum that marked the universe's heartbeat.

The eldest of the Starborn, Lumira, wove the Threads of Time and cast them across the newly formed heavens. These threads shimmered like silver strands, binding the tapestry together and setting the rhythm for the unfolding epochs. As time flowed, the tapestry pulsed with life, and fragments of the Great Void transformed into the vibrant lands and seas of Lanigami.

From Nagaía's breath came the winds of change, which spun the Starborn into a grand constellation. Each Starborn took its place in the Celestial Tapestry, defining the bounds of the cosmos. As the tapestry grew, the first hint of sound returned to the Void—a gentle hum that marked the universe's heartbeat.

The eldest of the Starborn, Lumira, wove the Threads of Time and cast them across the newly formed heavens. These threads shimmered like silver strands, binding the tapestry together and setting the rhythm for the unfolding epochs. As time flowed, the tapestry pulsed with life, and fragments of the Great Void transformed into the vibrant lands and seas of Lanigami.

In the center of this burgeoning world, Nagaía planted the Seed of Essence, a radiant gem that pulsed with the energy of creation itself. From this seed sprouted Yggalim, the World Tree, whose branches touched every corner of Lanigami. Its roots spread deep into the earth, while its leaves danced under the Starborn's eternal light, fostering life in infinite variety.

The children of Yggalim—the Faey, the Dāru, and the Elementals—arose from its embrace, each gifted with a unique essence drawn from the tree's vibrant aura. They explored the nascent world, shaping it with their dreams and desires, guided by the wisdom of Nagaía and the Starborn.

As Lanigami flourished, the Starborn descended from their celestial perch, taking physical forms to walk among the lands they helped create. They became the first Keepers, guiding the younger races and teaching them the art of harmony and balance.

Thus, the world of Lanigami was crafted—a realm of wonder and mystery, where the echoes of its creation continue to sing through valleys and streams, and every being remembers that they are but a part of Nagaía's eternal dance.

House rule: read every version, write one short note on each, say why, then mark the one to keep. Items 1 and 2 are done; item 3 is open.

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: The world of Brindle Quay is one of strange tales and histories.

In the beginning,

A. the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.
B. there was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
C. a smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

Notes:
A: Piled-up grandeur ('unvoiced hush', 'tremulous', 'resplendent'); little actually happens.
B: Small, odd, concrete: a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on a shrug.
C: A specific cause (melted anchors), a turn (the gulls answer), a human line at the end.
Why: C has a real reason for the bell and one line of character at the end; it is told, not announced.
Keep: C

A. the first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.
C. a woman left her porridge by the fire and forgot it. It rose and cracked and smelled like a promise. Her husband ate the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame.

A: An accident, a joke about the dead animal, one brave child.

A. there was no earth, no sky, and no sea—only a darkness so old it had forgotten what it was hiding.

Within that darkness slept a creature called Nami, whose body had no end. When Nami dreamed, its dreams became colors; when it stirred, those colors tangled together. But there was nothing to see them, and so they faded.

For an age beyond counting, Nami dreamed alone.

Then, one night—for nights existed before days—a dream refused to disappear.

It was a small, silver moth.

The moth settled upon Nami’s brow and asked, “Why do you make beautiful things only to lose them?”

“Because there is nowhere to keep them,” Nami answered.

“Then make somewhere.”

Nami opened one eye.

Where its gaze fell, the darkness hardened into stone. Where its breath passed, the stone softened into earth. It shook the dust from its skin, and the dust became stars. Yet the world lay cold and empty beneath them.

The moth flew downward and struck the earth with its wings.

From the first stroke came the mountains.

From the second came the forests.

From the third came every creature that walks, burrows, crawls, or hides beneath a leaf.

But with each stroke, the moth grew smaller.

Nami saw what was happening and wept. Its tears filled the valleys, making rivers and seas.

B. there was only the Great Void, an endless expanse of silence and stillness. From this nothingness emerged the Primordial Serpent, Nagaía, whose scales shimmered with the colors of all the worlds yet to be. Nagaía coiled through the Void, weaving dreams and possibilities with each graceful movement.

As Nagaía danced, her scales began to shed, and from each fallen scale, a Starborn emerged. These Starborn were the first beings of Lanigami, luminous entities composed of pure light and potential. They hovered in the darkness, whispering secrets to one another, their voices forming the first echoes of creation.

From Nagaía's breath came the winds of change, which spun the Starborn into a grand constellation. Each Starborn took its place in the Celestial Tapestry, defining the bounds of the cosmos. As the tapestry grew, the first hint of sound returned to the Void—a gentle hum that marked the universe's heartbeat.

The eldest of the Starborn, Lumira, wove the Threads of Time and cast them across the newly formed heavens. Within the Hush slept Ama-Ilun, the Dreamer. She had no shape, for no one had ever described her. She had no name, for no one had ever called

B. there was only the Fold—an infinite, shimmering plane of parchment-white void that bent and creased upon itself in endless silence. No stars burned. No waters stirred. There was only the quiet rustling of potential, like pages turning in an empty room.

From the deepest crease of the Fold, two beings emerged: **Orika**, who was shaped like an open hand, and **Suumeth**, who was shaped like a closed fist. They were not born, nor created—they simply *unfolded*, as if they had always existed within the material of the void, waiting only for the proper crease to reveal them.

Orika spoke first, and her voice was the sound of tearing. Where her words fell, the Fold ripped open, and from the wounds poured color—deep reds and burning golds and the blue-black of bruised sky. She laughed at what she had done, and her laughter made the tears spread wider, and the colors bled and pooled into what would become the seas and skies and molten hearts of mountains.

Suumeth did not speak. Instead, he pressed his closed fist against the Fold and *pushed*, compressing the void until it became dense and heavy and real. Where Orika tore open, Suumeth pressed together. From his pressure came stone and bone and iron. From his silence came gravity, the weight that taught all things to fall.

C. humans lived in a massive palace, only a wall, Aether or Void, separated them from the land. There humans built their palace and had their power. They gifted the Royal Guard his ring, to allow him to move back and forth between the palace and the core.

The Royal Guard was ordered to bring back the stone, said to take the form of a metal clay, black and slightly silver. It was no use, and when the Royal Guard returned to report, King Akarikazu was furious, and so the King and his Royal Guard changed through a portal to the other side of the wall, that separates Lanigami from The Realms of Concordia.

B. there was only the Fold—an infinite, shimmering plane of parchment-white void that bent and creased upon itself in endless silence. No stars burned. No waters stirred. There was only the quiet rustling of potential, like pages turning in an empty room.

From the deepest crease of the Fold, two beings emerged: **Orika**, who was shaped like an open hand, and **Suumeth**, who was shaped like a closed fist. They were not born, nor created—they simply *unfolded*, as if they had always existed within the material of the void, waiting only for the proper crease to reveal them.

Orika spoke first, and her voice was the sound of tearing. Where her words fell, the Fold ripped open, and from the wounds poured color—deep reds and burning golds and the blue-black of bruised sky. She laughed at what she had done, and her laughter made the tears spread wider, and the colors bled and pooled into what would become the seas and skies and molten hearts of mountains.

Suumeth did not speak. Instead, he pressed his closed fist against the Fold and *pushed*, compressing the void until it became dense and heavy and real. It is said that any soul could enter their palace, no matter what their status. However, when humans built their palace, they began to kill their own, until the last soldier of the Royal Guard killed the human king and allowed the entire population to move to the core of the capital. They gifted the Royal Guard his ring, to allow him to move back and forth between the palace and the core.

Long ago in Lanigami, King Akarikazu, ruler of all humans, ordered his Royal Guard to search for an ancient myth, said to take place on the small peninsula of Mount Aino in the east. The Royal Guard was ordered to bring back the stone, said to take the form of a metal clay, black and slightly silver. It was no use, and when the Royal Guard returned to report, King Akarikazu was furious, and so the King and his Royal Guard changed through a portal to the other side of the wall, that separates Lanigami from The Realms of Concordia.

The Royal Guard found the clay, and but in part it into his ring.

Over time, the Royal Guard was named, Diamond, and he experimented. He designed costumes, moving to the far west to build his kingdom of garb, and chipped away some of the blue jewel.

Their plan was to wake their brother Gombo and fool him into leaving his universe to go find them. Once he left, they could go take over his world. However, their plan backfired, and they arrived before their brother, finding himself bored and directionless. As the tapestry grew, the first hint of sound returned to the Void—a gentle hum that marked the universe's heartbeat.

These threads shimmered like silver strands, binding the tapestry together and setting the rhythm for the unfolding epochs. “Because there is nowhere to keep them,” Nami answered.

“Then make somewhere.”

The moth flew downward and struck the earth with its wings.

From the first stroke came the mountains.

From the second came the forests.

From the third came every creature that walks, burrows, crawls, or hides beneath a leaf.

But with each stroke, the moth grew smaller.

Nami saw what was happening and wept. Its tears filled the valleys, making rivers and seas.

It was no use, and when the Royal Guard returned to report, King Akarikazu was furious, and so the King and his Royal Guard changed through a portal to the other side of the wall, that separates Lanigami from The Realms of Concordia.

The Royal Guard found the clay, and but in part it into his ring.

Over time, the Royal Guard was named, Diamond, and he experimented. He designed costumes, moving to the far west to build his kingdom of garb, and chipped away some of the blue jewel.

D. three gods ruled over the world as supreme rulers. Gombo and Kagotsuch said they would create life in the clouds as only they could. Gombo created life in the ocean, as was fit for him. Saguchi would have made the life of the plants, but Gombo grew jealous and told Kagotsuch and Saguchi to go away.

And so they did. They left their master, alone, but not forgotten. Gombo created many people, but his jealousy caused his creations to become afraid and chaotic. In response, he grew angry, disorganized and developed a temper; all of which was reflected in his created world.

Saguchi and Kagotsuch were never satisfied with a life spent apart from their brothers. It was so empty. So lifeless. And so…

Their plan was to wake their brother Gombo and fool him into leaving his universe to go find them. Once he left, they could go take over his world. As the tapestry grew, the first hint of sound returned to the Void—a gentle hum that marked the universe's heartbeat.

The eldest of the Starborn, Lumira, wove the Threads of Time and cast them across the newly formed heavens. These threads shimmered like silver strands, binding the tapestry together and setting the rhythm for the unfolding epochs. As time flowed, the tapestry pulsed with life, and fragments of the Great Void transformed into the vibrant lands and seas of Lanigami.

They gifted the Royal Guard his ring, to allow him to move back and forth between the palace and the core.

The Royal Guard was ordered to bring back the stone, said to take the form of a metal clay, black and slightly silver. It was no use, and when the Royal Guard returned to report, King Akarikazu was furious, and so the King and his Royal Guard changed through a portal to the other side of the wall, that separates Lanigami from The Realms of Concordia.

The Royal Guard found the clay, and but in part it into his ring.

As time flowed, the tapestry pulsed with life, and fragments of the Great Void transformed into the vibrant lands and seas of Lanigami.

The moth flew downward and struck the earth with its wings.

From the first stroke came the mountains.

From the second came the forests.

From the third came every creature that walks, burrows, crawls, or hides beneath a leaf.

But with each stroke, the moth grew smaller.

Nami saw what was happening and wept. Its tears filled the valleys, making rivers and seas.

Which do you prefer? Reply with the letter on the first line, then one or two sentences on why.
instruct.text:
F
It has the strongest mythic voice and an emotional core: the moth's question gives creation a purpose, and its shrinking with each wingstroke adds a sense of sacrifice that makes the world feel earned. B comes close with its striking imagery, but F's simplicity and quiet poignancy feel more like a true creation myth.

It reads like a story passed down by firelight—each sentence lands with the unhurried, deliberate cadence of an oral tale, using simple declarative rhythms, intimate dialogue, and emotionally resonant images (the moth shrinking, Nami weeping into rivers) that feel discovered in the telling rather than constructed on the page.
